TauCetiRoadmap/FormalLaurentPuiseux:
# Formal Laurent fields, Puiseux expansions and continuous differential calculus

Develop formal substitution, continuous derivations and residues, finite ramified
Laurent extensions, the characteristic-zero Newton–Puiseux algebraic closure,
and its procyclic absolute Galois group. Supply usable coefficient, topology,
coordinate-change and finite-extension APIs for formal connections and loop
algebras.

## Carriers, scope and suppliers

Use Mathlib's `PowerSeries K`, `LaurentSeries K = HahnSeries ℤ K`,
`LaurentPolynomial K = AddMonoidAlgebra K ℤ`, and `HahnSeries ℚ K`.
K is an arbitrary field in L1–L4 except where characteristic zero is explicitly
required. L5's Newton-polygon and coprime-factor-Hensel APIs hold over arbitrary
K; its root theorem and L6–L7 assume characteristic zero and K algebraically
closed. Put `ord = HahnSeries.orderTop`, including ord(0)=∞;
ord(t)=1. Mathlib's multiplicative `LaurentSeries.valued` has v(t)=exp(−1).
Continuity on F=K((t)) always uses this valuation topology, with neighbourhoods
U_a=t^aK[[t]], a∈ℤ. Treat K as an algebraic coefficient field. A K-linear
functional to K is continuous precisely when it vanishes on some U_a; this
means a discrete codomain, independently of any other topology on K. For
ℂ((t)) use exactly this valuation topology.

Consume Mathlib's coefficient/order, power-series coercion, rational-function
embedding, valuation, completeness, Hasse derivative and `LaurentSeries.derivative`
APIs. Tau Ceti's `Huber.LaurentSeries.powerSeries_as_subring_eq_integer`,
`integers_powerSeries_as_subring` and `isOpen_powerSeries_as_subring` supply
existing valuation-ring results. Use `PowerSeries.subst`, `heval`,
`derivative_subst`, `subst_comp_subst` and `HahnSeries.embDomainAlgHom` for
substitution and exponent embeddings. Follow
[Mathlib PR #42313](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/pull/42313)'s
`LaurentSeries.expand (n : ℕ+)`, `contract (n : ℕ+) (f) (r : Fin n)`,
`sum_single_mul_expand_contract`, `contract_eq_of_sum_eq` and Hahn
`mem_range_embDomain_iff` shapes for ramified substitutions and the level basis.
Follow [PR #42471](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/pull/42471)'s
`hasseDeriv_mul` and `derivative_mul` in commutative-ring generality. Implement
required missing material in Tau Ceti in these shapes and adopt Mathlib's APIs
as they land. General algebraic closures, separability, Kummer theory and Krull
topology remain Mathlib's.

[AlgebraicCurves](../AlgebraicCurves/README.md) Layer 5 owns general complete-DVR
constructions; Layer 9 owns k-compatible place expansions and geometric residues
at places with finite separable residue extension. This roadmap owns the
coordinate-level calculus on Laurent-series carriers; transport its identities
along that roadmap's completion isomorphisms, including its residue-field trace.
The coefficient-level identities allow arbitrary fields K; geometric transport
includes the stated separability hypotheses. Compute ramification for
our explicit levels in L4/L6 directly from their exponent decomposition.
[ProfiniteArithmetic](../ProfiniteArithmetic/README.md) supplies the profinite
group `TauCeti.zHat`; its ring carrier is `Additive TauCeti.zHat`.

The Puiseux field is the subfield of `HahnSeries ℚ K` whose support has a single
positive common denominator: for some n>0, every supported exponent is k/n,
k∈ℤ. It is the union of embedded K((t^(1/n))) under divisibility transition
maps. Construct it on this carrier. Define `RamificationIndex` as a type
synonym of ℕ+ with order n≤m meaning n|m, independently of ℕ+'s usual order.
In L4 form the level diagram in `CommAlgCat K` on its thin category.
Prove there that its cocone into Puiseux is a colimit: every compatible family of
K-algebra maps into any commutative K-algebra factors uniquely through it.

[Dean Cureton's formal Puiseux development](https://github.com/deancureton/Puiseux)
constructs this directed-union carrier and proves algebraicity and algebraic
closedness (`PuiseuxSeries.isAlgClosure`). It is an existing implementation
candidate for L4–L5, independent of Tau Ceti's analytic Puiseux results. Coordinate
with its author before integrating code, following this repository's porting
policy. The targets below specify the mathematics whether developed independently
or integrated; retain their full coefficient, topology, differential and Galois
APIs rather than stopping at the closure theorem.

## L1. Formal substitutions and coordinate groups

Expose the constant-field, polynomial, power-series and Laurent-field maps as
a compatible algebra tower. Construct the Laurent-polynomial embedding by
its finite sum of monomials. Prove injectivity, coefficient formulas, image
and order characterizations. Identify K[[t]] with the nonnegative-order
valuation ring, its maximal ideal with positive order and residue with constant
coefficient. Prove Laurent-polynomial density and truncation convergence:
f_i→f iff for every a, eventually ord(f_i−f)≥a. Equivalently, the supports
are eventually uniformly bounded below and each coefficient eventually equals
the corresponding coefficient of f. Prove this by stabilization of the finite
interval between the support bound and a. The sequence t^(−j), j≥1, has
coefficientwise eventual zero but fails valuation convergence.

For every nonzero φ∈tK[[t]] construct substitution on K[[t]] and extend to F
using f=t^(−N)f₊. Prove independence of N, K-algebra-map laws, composition,
injectivity and ord(f(φ))=ord(φ)ord(f) for f≠0. Supply continuity, coefficient
formulas and the ramified substitution t↦s^e, e>0, between two copies of F.

Coordinates are those φ with nonzero linear coefficient. Give K[[t]] the
subspace valuation topology from F through a scoped instance in a named namespace,
with its inclusion into F an `IsInducing` map. Keep this scope distinct from
`PowerSeries.WithPiTopology`; introduce no global topology instance. Construct their
K-algebra automorphism group of K[[t]] with multiplication σ·τ=σ∘τ.
Writing σ_φ(f)=f(φ), pin σ_φ∘σ_ψ=σ_(ψ(φ)); thus the parameter-series
composition group maps anti-isomorphically to this automorphism group.
Construct inverses and prove this parameter dictionary. Prove such automorphisms preserve the maximal ideal
and are automatically continuous. Obtain inverse coefficients recursively:
the degree-n composition equation determines b_n by the nonzero linear term,
and prove uniqueness. For each N≥1 define the N-jet group as these substitutions
modulo t^(N+1), give composition and truncation maps, and prove the full group
is their inverse limit, with the jet groups discrete and the coordinate group
given the topology of agreement modulo each t^(N+1). Define infinitesimal substitutions as K[ε]-algebra automorphisms of
`PowerSeries (DualNumber K)`, reducing to identity and preserving (t); identify their ε-coefficients with
tK[[t]]D. Prove every K-derivation K[[t]]→K[[t]] is t-adically continuous:
δ(t^n f)=nt^(n−1)fδ(t)+t^nδ(f) gives δ((t^n))⊆(t^(n−1)).
Truncation then determines δ from δ(t), including in positive characteristic. Over `DualNumber (DualNumber K)`, identified with
K[ε₁,ε₂]/(ε₁²,ε₂²), with σ₁=1+ε₁aD and σ₂=1+ε₂bD,
prove σ₁σ₂σ₁⁻¹σ₂⁻¹=1+ε₁ε₂(aDb−bDa)D. This pins the operator-commutator
sign. For every coefficient-field embedding K→K′, use coefficientwise
power/Laurent maps and prove naturality of substitution and jet truncation.

## L2. Continuous derivations and one-forms

Prove product, inverse and quotient rules for the existing Laurent derivative
D, compatibility with power-series derivatives and Hasse derivatives, and the
chain rule for all L1 substitutions. Prove ord(Df)≥ord(f)−1 and continuity.
For f≠0 with leading exponent r and coefficient a_r≠0, if r has nonzero
image in K prove coeff_(r−1)(Df)=r a_r and ord(Df)=r−1. When that image vanishes, locate the first
exponent with nonzero differentiated coefficient, or prove Df=0. In
characteristic zero prove ker D=K.

Use Mathlib's `Derivation K F F`; take the submodule of maps continuous for the
valuation topology. Prove each is uniquely aD, a∈F, and conversely every aD is
continuous. Prove bracket closure and [aD,bD]=(aDb−bDa)D. Characterize the
K[[t]]-preserving and maximal-ideal-preserving subalgebras as respectively
K[[t]]D and tK[[t]]D, with the L1 infinitesimal-coordinate comparison.

Package D as a `Derivation K F F` using its product rule.
Let λ:Ω[F/K]→F be `D.liftKaehlerDifferential`. Define Ω¹_cont(F/K) as
Ω[F/K]/ker λ and prove the induced F-linear equivalence with F, sending dt
to 1. Give it the transported valuation module topology. For a finite-dimensional
Hausdorff F-module M with `IsModuleTopology F M`, prove continuous K-derivations F→M
factor uniquely through this quotient by a continuous F-linear map. Establish
continuity of factorization and of the quotient derivation. The construction factors the algebraic Kähler derivation through the
specified quotient, identifying its dt class with 1.
Prove coordinate covariance du=Dφ dt, functoriality and compatibility with
coefficientwise field embeddings K→K′;
for coordinate automorphisms this gives an invertible semilinear map on forms.

## L3. Residue, primitives and coefficient duality

Define Res(f dt)=coeff_(−1) f. Prove linearity, vanishing on U_0 dt,
Res(dg)=0 and Res(f dg)=−Res(g df). Prove for every nonzero φ∈tK[[t]] of
order e the finite-map formula Res(f(φ)Dφ dt)=e Res(f dt), in all
characteristics. In particular coordinate changes preserve residue. Build the
universal coefficient identity, for a commutative ring R, a unit u∈R[[t]]ˣ
and e,k≥1:

`e·coeff_(ek)(u^(−k)) + coeff_(ek−1)(u^(−k−1)u′) = 0`.

Prove inverse/product/derivative compatibility with `PowerSeries.map` and
finite-jet dependence of these coefficients. In the universal ring
ℤ[x₀,…,x_(ek)][x₀⁻¹], prove the identity by passage to its characteristic-zero
fraction field and injectivity, then specialize x_j to the coefficients of u
in R. For φ=t^e u this treats all negative monomials except t^(−1), whose
residue is e; nonnegative monomials have zero residue. Extend by valuation
continuity. AlgebraicCurves Layer 9 transports this coordinate-level formula
along its completion charts.

In characteristic zero construct a primitive of every residue-zero form by
termwise division, prove uniqueness modulo K, and characterize im D as exactly
these forms. Include negative exponents and the excluded t^(−1) coefficient.
The t^(−1) form remains outside the derivative image.

Prove nondegeneracy of (f,g)↦Res(fg dt), annihilator(U_a)=U_(−a), and perfect
finite-dimensional pairings U_a/U_b × U_(−b)/U_(−a), a≤b. For finite-dimensional
K-vector spaces V use `HahnModule ℤ K V` for V((t)) with its F-module action,
and the coefficient-preserving `HahnModule.of` comparison to `LaurentSeries V`.
Topologize it by the K-linear lattices U_a=t^aV[[t]], consisting of series
with every coefficient below a zero; these are K[[t]]-submodules. Prove the natural F-linear comparison F⊗_K V≃V((t)) for finite-dimensional V,
using the singleton constant-coefficient map; prove finite-basis independence,
completeness and the power-series lattice/finite-jet comparisons. Identify its
continuous K-linear dual with V*((t))dt by coefficient contraction and residue.
Define the dual topology by annihilators of U_(−a)(V); prove this identification
is a homeomorphism and compatible with linear maps. The dt factor gives the
coordinate-covariant description; changing parameters transforms forms too.

Compare Laurent-polynomial derivative/residue with the Laurent embedding.
For every K-Lie algebra L, construct the K-linear map
`AddMonoidAlgebra K ℤ ⊗[K] L → HahnModule ℤ K L` sending t^j⊗v to the
coefficient-j singleton v. Define the bracket directly by coefficient
convolution on `HahnModule ℤ K L` for every K-Lie algebra L; prove the
coefficient sums finite and the support bounded below, and establish the Lie
identities over K. For finite-dimensional L give F⊗_K L its scalar-extended
F-Lie algebra and L((t)) its coefficientwise F-action, then prove the
comparison is an F-`LieEquiv`. Transport `LaurentSeries.derivative K` on `LaurentSeries L`
through `HahnModule.of` to define D on L((t)); prove continuity and
D(f·v)=Df·v+f·Dv. Prove coefficient formulas, injectivity, bracket compatibility and
functoriality. Extend a K-bilinear form Φ coefficientwise
and prove that Res(Φ(f,Dg)dt), restricted along this polynomial-loop embedding,
is Mathlib's `LieAlgebra.LoopAlgebra.residuePairing Φ`, including
its coefficient n on a second argument of degree n. These are the exact
supplier identities for formal loop cocycles.

## L4. Ramified levels and the Puiseux field

For n>0 construct ι_n:K((u))→K⟦ℚ⟧ using `HahnSeries.embDomainAlgHom` on
k↦k/n, with coefficient, support and injectivity theorems. For n|m construct
u_n↦u_m^(m/n), prove composition and compatibility with ι_n and ι_m.
Identify level-n images by denominator n, intersections by gcd, and generated
composita by lcm. Prove every finite family of Puiseux elements lies in a
single common level, with a common-level lift for polynomial coefficients.
Prove closure of their union under addition, multiplication and inverse, and install the resulting subfield's K- and level-one F-algebra
structures with the tower laws.

Over F, prove level n has basis 1,u,…,u^(n−1): split an arbitrary Laurent
series into its n exponent congruence classes and prove uniqueness. Thus its
degree is n and every Puiseux element is algebraic over F in all
characteristics. Identify the level with adjoining a root of X^n−t, and prove
irreducibility by this basis or the valuation-ring Eisenstein/Gauss argument.
Supply the substitution comparison to L1's t↦u^n.

Restrict `HahnSeries.addVal` to obtain the Puiseux additive valuation in
`WithTop ℚ`, and compare with each level's integer order scaled by 1/n.
Supply its multiplicative valuation in `WithZero (Multiplicative ℚ)`, sending
a nonzero series of order q to `WithZero.exp (−q)` and zero to zero;
use its valuation topology and prove level
embeddings are homeomorphisms onto their images. Prove the Puiseux field is
not complete: the partial sums of Σ_(j≥1) t^(j+1/(j+1)) are Puiseux elements
and form a valuation-Cauchy sequence, while its Hahn-series limit has no finite
common denominator. Prove coefficient uniqueness excludes any Puiseux limit.
This also exhibits its strict inclusion in the full rational Hahn field.

In characteristic zero define D_t on this subfield by the coefficient rule
D_t(t^q)=q t^(q−1). Prove its support remains at a finite level, level
compatibility, continuity and product/chain identities. Under ι_n,
D_t(ι_n f)=(1/n)u^(1−n)ι_n(D_u f). Define one-forms by the same continuous
quotient construction at each level, with compatible transition maps.
With dt=n u^(n−1)du prove Res_u(f dt)=n Res_t(f dt), where Res_t on Puiseux
means rational-exponent coefficient −1. Prove its residue-zero primitive
criterion and coordinate/substitution comparisons.

## L5. Newton polygons and formal Newton–Puiseux

For polynomials over F construct coefficient Newton polygons, faces/slopes and
initial polynomials. Supply translation, scaling, the Minkowski-sum formula for
Newton polygons of nonzero products (equivalently union of slope multisets), coefficient
valuation bounds and ramified-substitution APIs. Consume the existing
`IsAdicComplete.henselianRing`/simple-root Hensel theorem for K[[t]], proving
the reduction hypotheses needed. Consume the existing instance
`IsAdicComplete (Ideal.span {PowerSeries.X}) (PowerSeries K)` and compare that
ideal to the maximal ideal. Build the monic
coprime-factor lifting theorem as an explicit target: from a factorization
of the reduction into coprime monic factors, lift uniquely to monic factors
of the same degrees. Give the recursive coefficient correction by Bézout and
polynomial division, prove coefficientwise compatibility and completeness,
and compare its degree-one specialization to the existing simple-root theorem.

For algebraically closed K of characteristic zero prove every nonconstant
polynomial over F has a root at a finite L4 level. Normalize to monic and clear
poles by scaling the unknown. At a monic polynomial of degree m, remove its
degree-(m−1) coefficient by a Tschirnhaus shift. Write the translated
polynomial as P=Y^m+Σ_(i=2)^m a_i Y^(m−i). If every a_i=0, the root is
zero; otherwise choose the minimum ord(a_i)/i over its nonzero coefficients a_i,
ramify t=s^q to clear that slope's denominator, rescale Y=s^p Z and divide
by s^(pm). Prove the transformed polynomial is monic over K[[s]], still has
zero degree-(m−1) coefficient, and its reduction has a nonzero lower term.
Its reduction therefore cannot be (Z−a)^m: for a≠0 the coefficient −ma
is nonzero in characteristic zero, and for a=0 it has no lower term. Choose
a nonzero root and split off its multiplicity-r factor, with 0<r<m and
coprime complement. Apply the specified factor-Hensel target to obtain a
monic degree-r factor and recurse. Termination is strict degree descent.
Track all substitution/inverse transformations and finite ramification levels;
the final degree-one factor gives a root in one complete level. Include
polynomials with repeated roots and negative slopes after Laurent normalization. The
coprime-factor lifting theorem and polynomial transformations are built before
this degree induction.

For a polynomial over Puiseux, first lift its finite coefficient family to one
common level from L4, reinterpret that level as K((u)), apply the root theorem
there, and compare the resulting level-nm embedding to the original Hahn
carrier. Deduce splitting, algebraic closedness and identification of the
Puiseux field as an algebraic closure of F using L4's finite-degree algebraicity.
Include polynomials with repeated roots and nonmonic polynomials. Examples must compute X^n−t,
fractional leading orders and distinct branches with a common initial term.
The sharp minimal-level bound and the resulting degree-factorial bound are L6
targets following the finite-extension classification.

## L6. Finite extensions, trace and compatible roots

Assume K algebraically closed of characteristic zero. Use L4's degree-n root
adjunction and Mathlib's `autEquivRootsOfUnity`, `autEquivZmod` and
`isGalois_of_isSplittingField_X_pow_sub_C` after identifying level n as the
splitting field of X^n−t. Prove the Kummer action u↦ζu, restriction formulas
and fixed fields on the actual Hahn-level carrier, consuming generic Kummer
and Galois correspondence rather than rebuilding them.

Every finite extension embeds in a level by L5 and finite generation. Prove
it is isomorphic over F to K((t^(1/e))) by cyclic Galois correspondence. These
are chosen AlgEquiv maps between field constructions. Compute the residue
field K, ramification index e, integer ring and valuation comparisons directly
from their exponent decomposition; no finite-residue hypothesis is used.
For a root α of a degree-d polynomial its minimal level equals [F(α):F]≤d,
so α lies at a level dividing d!, and all roots can be placed at level d!.

Construct trace on differentials via Ω¹_cont(L/K)=L⊗_F Ω¹_cont(F/K), prove
this equivalence for the finite separable level map, and prove
Res_F(Tr_(L/F) ω)=Res_L(ω). Verify the formula on u-monomials and extend by
continuity. Prove that the finite-extension residue is independent of the chosen
F-algebra equivalence with K((u)): compare its parameter-root images, then use
L3 coordinate invariance. State the corollaries
Res_F(Tr_(L_e/F)ω)=e Res_t^ℚ(ω) and Res_(u_m)=(m/n)Res_(u_n) under n|m,
while Res_t^ℚ is compatible with the Hahn transition inclusions. Distinguish the coefficient-−1 Res_t on rational exponents from
Res_u: the latter includes the factor e when a form is expressed with dt.

Construct primitive roots ζ_n∈K for every n>0, compatible by
ζ_m^(m/n)=ζ_n when n|m, and prove existence. For K=ℂ use exp(2πi/n).
Use a fresh type synonym for each finite group μ_n(K) and give it the
discrete topology, independently of any topology on K or its units. Construct
the inverse limit in `ProfiniteGrp` of these finite discrete groups, with
transition ζ↦ζ^(m/n), as their compatible-family closed subgroup of the
product. Prove its profinite structure, and construct the induced compatible
coefficientwise action on every Puiseux level, faithfulness and fixed fields.

## L7. Absolute Galois topology and parameter independence

Use Mathlib's Krull-topology carriers and
`InfiniteGalois.continuousMulEquivToLimit` on the L5 algebraic closure.
Prove the ramified levels are cofinal among finite Galois intermediate fields,
and give the cofinal-limit comparison to L6's μ_n limit. Consume Mathlib's
compactness/Hausdorff and inverse-limit theorems. Identify finite-level
stabilizers and transport to Mathlib's chosen `AlgebraicClosure F` through a
chosen F-algebra equivalence. Prove that the induced Galois-group comparison
and normalized generator are independent of this choice: two choices differ
by a Galois automorphism, and conjugation is trivial by L6's abelian group.

The compatible roots define the automorphism σ_ζ by u_n↦ζ_n u_n. Use
`TauCeti.zHat.lift σ_ζ` into the profinite Galois group. Consume
`zHat.lift_surjective` and `lift_injective_of_finite_quotients`, proving their
generator/detection hypotheses using the finite-level coordinates and obtain inverse continuity by compact-to-T2.
Thus Gal(F)≃ₜ*TauCeti.zHat with the generator sent to σ_ζ. Changing the
primitive-root system changes this coordinate by a unit of the profinite
integer ring; consume `TauCeti.zHat.existsUnique_forall_toZMod_eq`,
`TauCeti.zpowHat_eq_pow_val_toZMod` and `TauCeti.zHat.unitsLift` for the
compatible finite-level coordinates, exponent action and unit comparison.
Prove the action and inverse formulas.

Prove every unit in K[[t]] has an n-th root there, for n>0, using its constant
root and simple-root Hensel. Consequently the character
θ_n(g)=g(π^(1/n))/π^(1/n) is independent of the chosen uniformizer π and
of its chosen n-th root. Prove compatibility in n. A K-linear formal parameter
automorphism lifts to the algebraic closure; any two lifts induce the same
conjugation on the abelian Galois group, and this conjugation is identity by
the θ_n comparisons. The whole absolute Galois group is inertia here. Only
the identification with the specified generator of zHat uses ζ.

## Order and boundaries

L1→L2→L3 is independent of Newton–Puiseux. L4's embeddings and basis depend
on L1; its differential refinement uses L2–L3 and characteristic zero.
L5→L6→L7 follows that finite-level foundation. Every new object has
extensionality, composition, transport and its coefficient/topology formulas
before use downstream.

Positive-characteristic algebraic-closure descriptions, mixed-characteristic
local fields, analytic branch convergence, Stokes data, formal connections,
opers, affine central extensions and categorical Langlands statements are
outside this roadmap's scope. Tau Ceti's analytic Puiseux results concern analytic branch convergence and
have their own analytic hypotheses.

## References

- [Frenkel, *Langlands Correspondence for Loop Groups*](https://math.berkeley.edu/~frenkel/loop.pdf),
  §1.2, for the formal Laurent/Puiseux and local-parameter setting.
- [Mannaa–Coquand, *Dynamic Newton–Puiseux Theorem*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1304.6770),
  §1, for the centered-polynomial, ramification and factor-Hensel proof route.
- [Mathlib Kummer theory](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/6b7abb3c7686292736be2955bd3eb9ebf63b456a/Mathlib/FieldTheory/KummerExtension.lean)
  and [profinite Galois comparison](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/6b7abb3c7686292736be2955bd3eb9ebf63b456a/Mathlib/FieldTheory/Galois/Profinite.lean).
- [Formal versus convergent Puiseux discussion](https://leanprover.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/287929-mathlib4/topic/Remaining.20100.20theorems/near/484400866)
  for the distinction from analytic branch convergence.
TauCetiRoadmap/GeometricMeasureTheory:
# Geometric measure theory: rectifiability, BV, and finite perimeter

Build a reusable Euclidean geometric measure theory library through the structure theorem for
sets of finite perimeter, area and coarea, approximation, compactness, traces, and Gauss–Green.
These results supply the measure-theoretic foundation for
[Euclidean isoperimetry](../Isoperimetry/README.md), including its sharp inequality and ball rigidity.
The objects must support further analysis independently of that application: restriction,
localization, a.e. equivalence, change of variables, and comparisons with classical calculus are
part of their basic theory.

The scope is finite-dimensional real Euclidean spaces, with metric curve results in the greater
generality their statements permit. Currents, varifolds, and regularity theory for minimizing
hypersurfaces are outside this roadmap. All the milestones below are required.
[Suggested.lean](Suggested.lean) illustrates some interfaces; this README is definitive.

## Conventions and ownership

- Use `EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n)` and intrinsic finite-dimensional real inner-product spaces,
  with `volume` for Lebesgue measure. Transfer results by linear isometry equivalences rather
  than developing coordinate-specific theories. In dimension two include the existing real
  inner-product space `ℂ`.
- For set theorems, Lebesgue measurability means `NullMeasurableSet E volume`; use
  `MeasurableSet` for a Borel representative and transfer by equality a.e. The full perimeter
  theory must accommodate all Lebesgue measurable representatives, including null
  modifications of Borel sets.
- **Hausdorff measure is the normalized Euclidean measure**
  [`MeasureTheory.Measure.euclideanHausdorffMeasure`](https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/Geometry/Euclidean/Volume/Measure.html#MeasureTheory.Measure.euclideanHausdorffMeasure),
  written `μHE[k]`. It agrees with `volume` on a `k`-dimensional Euclidean space. Write
  `Hᵏ` for this measure below. Retain explicit comparison lemmas with Mathlib's raw Hausdorff
  measure. Do not silently exchange the two normalizations.
- A rectifiable parameterized curve is a continuous map on a compact real interval with
  `BoundedVariationOn`; its length is the existing `eVariationOn`. No new path or length
  carrier replaces Mathlib's maps, `Path`, or total variation. Use extended nonnegative
  quantities first; conversion to real length requires a finiteness theorem.
- A countably `k`-rectifiable set is covered, up to an `Hᵏ`-null set, by countably many
  Lipschitz images of subsets of `ℝᵏ`. Distinguish this from finite `Hᵏ` measure and from
  parameterized rectifiability. State measurability separately where it is needed.
- For real-valued functions on Euclidean open sets, `BV_loc(Ω)` means a locally integrable
  function whose distributional
  derivative is a locally finite vector-valued Radon measure. `BV(Ω)` additionally requires
  integrability and finite total variation. Use the distributional identity
  `∫ u div φ = −∫ φ · dDu` for smooth compactly supported vector fields in `Ω`.
  Derivatives and variation are invariant under equality a.e. on `Ω`.
- Define extended perimeter for every measurable set by the supremum of
  `∫_E div φ` over smooth vector fields compactly supported in the open set `Ω`, with
  pointwise norm at most one. A set has locally finite perimeter when its indicator
  belongs to `BV_loc`. Its perimeter measure is `|Dχ_E|`, and the supremum agrees with
  `P(E; Ω) = |Dχ_E|(Ω)` whenever that measure exists. Finite perimeter on the
  whole space means `P(E; univ) < ∞`; it does **not** require finite volume. Global `BV`
  membership of the indicator additionally requires finite volume. Complements must have
  the same perimeter.
- The outward measure-theoretic unit normal has sign
  `Dχ_E = −ν_E Hⁿ⁻¹|∂*E`. Distinguish topological frontier, essential boundary, and reduced
  boundary. The last two are measure-theoretic notions, with statements independent of
  the chosen a.e. representative.

[PDE](../PDE/README.md), Lane A.1–A.3, owns weak-derivative Sobolev spaces and their smooth
density and Fourier comparisons. Extend the actual `TauCeti.HasWeakFDerivOn` and `W1p`
APIs to measure-valued derivatives; prove the comparison rather than inventing another weak
derivative. Its Lane A.5–A.6 owns Sobolev Poincaré, domain traces, extensions, and Rellich.
This roadmap owns BV versions and their agreement with those Sobolev results.

[ConformalMapping](../ConformalMapping/README.md), L5, owns Jordan separation and the
filled-hull topology. [DifferentialGeometry](../DifferentialGeometry/README.md), whose
[Green layer 5.6 targets](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/pull/826) specify
the flat planar extension, owns
winding numbers, planar curve integrals, and Green's area identity. This roadmap owns metric
length, arclength, rectifiability, and Hausdorff measure comparisons. The sharp Euclidean
isoperimetric constants, Brunn–Minkowski, rearrangements, and ball rigidity belong to
[Isoperimetry](../Isoperimetry/README.md). The nonsharp local estimate in G4 below is a
foundation for perimeter structure, not a dependency on that sharp theorem.

## Existing floor and API design

Consume Mathlib's Hausdorff measures, Radon measures, signed and vector measures, total
variation, Radon–Nikodym and Lebesgue decomposition, Bochner integration, Rademacher and
change of variables, and the calculus of test functions. Tau Ceti supplies
`TauCeti.metricDerivative`, its a.e. existence and integrable distance bound for
absolutely continuous curves, the `C¹` variation–speed identity in
`TauCeti.Analysis.Calculus.MetricVariation`, weak derivatives, and `W1p`. G1 extends these
curve results; G2–G3 build the remaining measure and derivative bridges.

Use [`LinearMap.normDet`](https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/Analysis/InnerProductSpace/NormDet.html#LinearMap.normDet)
and its continuous-linear-map version for geometric Jacobians. Mathlib already relates it
to Gram determinants and the volume of linear images; do not introduce another Jacobian
for rectangular linear maps. In particular, consume
`LinearMap.euclideanHausdorffMeasure_image_eq_normDet_mul_volume` for linear images.
For the coarea Jacobian of a map from dimension `n` to `m ≤ n`,
use the norm determinant of its adjoint. Prove the chart and tangent-space comparison lemmas
needed for the nonlinear formulas.

Follow the API direction of these Mathlib proposals and discussions, implementing missing
results in Tau Ceti without waiting for them:

- [Arclength continuity, mathlib4#31766](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/pull/31766):
  cumulative variation and continuity for continuous rectifiable curves.
- [Finite variation of finite-dimensional vector measures, #42103](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/pull/42103):
  vector-measure variation, used by G2–G3.
- [Connected sets of finite Hausdorff length, #41839](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/pull/41839):
  diameter and length comparisons, used by G1.
- [Uniformly distributed measures, #37310](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/pull/37310)
  and the [Hausdorff/coarea discussion](https://leanprover.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/217875-Is%20there%20code%20for%20X%3F/topic/Finding%20n-dimensional%20polar%20coordinate%20formula%20for%20sobolev.):
  normalized Hausdorff measure, sphere measures, and polar integration. G2 requires the
  actual sphere-measure comparison, not merely a uniqueness theorem that could prove it.

## G1 — Rectifiable curves and arclength

Consume the existing variation API: `eVariationOn.mono`, `Icc_add_Icc`,
`comp_eq_of_antitoneOn`, `comp_eq_of_monotoneOn`, `lowerSemicontinuous_uniformOn`, and
`edist_le`, together with Tau Ceti's `eVariationOn_le_liminf_of_eventually_le`. Use the
`TauCeti.IsCurveJoining`/`Path` comparison in `Topology/MetricSpace/Length.lean` where a
joining curve is required. Build the curve-specific concatenation and restriction
comparisons not already expressed by those APIs. Build cumulative arclength,
prove its continuity and endpoint values, and factor a rectifiable curve through a
unit-speed Lipschitz curve on its length interval. Handle constant pieces by factorization;
an inverse of the cumulative arclength function is not available for a general curve.
For injective arcs, give the strictly increasing reparametrization and its homeomorphism.
For closed curves injective except at the endpoints, give an arclength parametrization
with that same simplicity property. Include zero-length cases explicitly.

For absolutely continuous curves prove length equals the integral of the metric derivative.
In finite-dimensional real normed spaces identify it a.e. with the norm of the vector derivative and
deduce `eVariationOn γ = ∫⁻ ‖γ'‖`. Supply the interval-integral real-valued form with its
integrability and finite-length hypotheses. Relate the factorization to the FTC and prove
that a nonconstant arclength parametrization has speed one a.e. Reconcile these statements
with existing `C¹` and `Path` APIs.

Prove `H¹(trace γ) ≤ length γ`, with equality for injective arcs and simple closed curves
(endpoints identified). Conversely, a continuous injective arc or simple closed curve
with finite `H¹` trace has finite variation. Prove this using partitions, the connected-set
diameter bound, and additivity of trace measure; it must not assume a Lipschitz input
parameter. Thus finite geometric length and parameterized rectifiability agree for these
curves. Include the multiplicity formula supplied by G2 for nonsimple
curves, so a twice-traversed circle has twice the variation length and the same trace
measure. Deduce that rectifiable planar traces have zero two-dimensional volume.
Make all length identities invariant under increasing continuous onto reparametrizations.
DifferentialGeometry's [rectifiable-curve interface](../DifferentialGeometry/README.md#rectifiable-curves-and-geometric-measure-theory)
consumes this arclength factorization to construct geometric
line integrals and their orientation/parametrization comparisons. G1 does not use those
integral comparisons as an input to the metric theory.

The variation, factorization, upper length bound, and exact comparisons for injective arcs
and simple closed curves are G1 targets independent of G2, using partitions and the
connected-set diameter bound for the lower comparison. The multiplicity formula for
nonsimple curves follows G2's one-dimensional area formula. G2 does not assume that
multiplicity formula in its proof.

## G2 — Rectifiability, area, and coarea

Build the closure and transport API for countably rectifiable sets: measurable restrictions,
countable unions, null modifications, Lipschitz images, and isometries. For countably
`k`-rectifiable sets with locally finite `Hᵏ` measure prove existence and a.e. uniqueness
of approximate tangent `k`-planes,
measurability of the tangent-plane field, and the density theorem. Build tangential
differentiation for Lipschitz maps on these sets and show independence of charts and null
modifications. Prove agreement with tangent spaces and surface Jacobians on `C¹` graphs.

Prove the **area formula** for Lipschitz maps `f : ℝᵐ → ℝⁿ`, `m ≤ n`, on measurable sets,
with nonnegative measurable weights:

```
∫_A g(x) J_m f(x) dx = ∫_{ℝⁿ} Σ_{x ∈ A ∩ f⁻¹{y}} g(x) dHᵐ(y).
```

Multiplicity is an extended nonnegative count, with measurable weighted fiber sums; do
not use a finite-cardinality convention that returns zero for infinite fibers. Supply the
injective specialization and finite-dimensional isometric transport. Derive the tangential
area formula for maps on countably rectifiable sets.

Prove the **coarea formula** for Lipschitz `f : ℝⁿ → ℝᵐ`, `m ≤ n`, with the same weighted
generality, integrating `Hⁿ⁻ᵐ` over fibers and Lebesgue measure in the target. Include the
fiber measurability, a.e. rectifiability, and exceptional-set statements the formula needs.
Give real integrable versions after proving finiteness. The differentiability, covering,
measurability, and approximation lemmas needed for these formulas are themselves targets
of G2, using Mathlib's Rademacher theorem rather than presuming nonlinear area or coarea.

Derive graph surface measure, spherical surface measure, polar integration, and slicing by
linear projections. Prove `Hⁿ⁻¹(sphere c r) = n ω_n r^(n−1)` for `n ≥ 1`, `r > 0`, where
`ω_n = volume(ball 0 1)`, and the unit-sphere comparison with angular measure. Normalize
`H⁰` as counting measure. These identities must agree with existing ball volume and
linear-image formulas; they provide the actual constants used by isoperimetry.

## G3 — Distributional BV and variation measures

Construct the measure-valued derivative, its uniqueness, and its total variation from the
test-function identity. Prove equivalence with the local variational characterization
using compactly supported smooth vector fields with pointwise norm at most one. Establish
the Radon representation and its localization on arbitrary open subsets, using Mathlib's
Riesz representation and vector-measure infrastructure and building every missing bridge.
Handle locally finite derivatives on unbounded domains by compatible restrictions; do not
assume a globally finite vector measure at the definition of `BV_loc`.

Give the unbundled a.e.-invariant predicate and the normed a.e.-quotient `BV(Ω)` with norm
`‖u‖₁ + |Du|(Ω)`. Prove completeness, restriction, scalar multiplication, addition, lattice
operations, multiplication by smooth cutoffs, Lipschitz scalar composition and its variation
bound, affine isometric transport, and scaling by positive dilations. For global BV
composition require integrability of the composite, obtained for example from `φ(0)=0`;
local BV has no such whole-space integrability requirement. Supply the polar decomposition
`Du = σ_u |Du|`, with `‖σ_u‖ = 1` a.e., and the absolutely continuous/singular decomposition.
Do not apply the classical chain rule across jumps: composition results must give the
correct BV identity or a variation inequality.

Compare with `TauCeti.HasWeakFDerivOn` and `W1p`: a `W¹,¹` function is BV, its derivative
measure has weak gradient as density, and its variation is the integral of the gradient
norm. Conversely an integrable BV function with an absolutely continuous derivative is
`W¹,¹`. Include the local versions and the one-dimensional comparison with classical
variation and the derivative measure of a BV function. Prove measure-valued integration
by parts and agreement with smooth calculus.

## G4 — Approximation, compactness, and scalar coarea

Prove lower semicontinuity of variation under local `L¹` convergence, weak convergence of
the derivative measures under locally bounded variation, and compactness in `L¹_loc` for
families locally bounded in `L¹` and variation. For bounded Lipschitz domains derive global
`L¹` compactness under a global BV bound. Establish convolution estimates, local smooth
approximation on arbitrary open sets by a partition of unity, and **strict approximation**:
`u_j → u` in `L¹` and `|Du_j|(Ω) → |Du|(Ω)`.

Prove scalar BV coarea on open sets:

```
|Du|(Ω) = ∫_{ℝ} P({x | u(x) > t}; Ω) dt.
```

The superlevel sets have locally finite perimeter for a.e. `t`; provide their measurable
dependence on `t`, the local measure identity, layer-cake formulas, truncation formulas,
and the converse characterization. Derive approximation of finite-volume finite-perimeter
sets by bounded smooth sets with volume convergence and perimeter convergence on the whole
space. Build cutoff/truncation and regular-level arguments. Consume
`TauCeti.addHaar_image_criticalPoints_eq_zero` from
`TauCeti.Analysis.Calculus.Sard.OutermostStratum` in the smooth scalar regime: its finite
regularity threshold is automatically met by `C∞` functions. Build the regular-level and
level-set boundary comparisons needed for the approximation from that theorem. Do not strengthen
this to preservation of equality cases under approximation.

Supply BV Poincaré on balls and the nonsharp relative perimeter estimate

```
min(|E ∩ B_r|, |B_r \ E|)^((n−1)/n) ≤ C_n P(E; B_r),    n ≥ 2,
```

for locally finite-perimeter sets and `r > 0`, with a positive constant depending only on
`n`, plus scaling and localization. Consume Mathlib's compactly supported `C¹` estimate
`MeasureTheory.eLpNorm_le_eLpNorm_fderiv_one`; build its BV and local-domain extensions,
and the covering estimates needed for this result here, without using the
sharp theorem in Isoperimetry. This is the analytic input for G5's boundary structure.

## G5 — Finite perimeter and boundary structure

Build the usable perimeter API: a.e. invariance, complements, locality, relative perimeter,
unions/intersections with the submodularity inequality, truncation by balls, scaling,
isometries, smooth approximation, compactness, and lower semicontinuity. Distinguish finite
perimeter from finite volume in every theorem.

Define measure-theoretic density, essential interior/exterior, essential boundary, reduced
boundary, and outward normal. Prove the Lebesgue density facts and **De Giorgi's structure
theorem**: the reduced boundary is countably `(n−1)`-rectifiable, its blow-up is an oriented
half-space at `Hⁿ⁻¹`-a.e. point, and

```
|Dχ_E| = Hⁿ⁻¹|∂*E,       Dχ_E = −ν_E Hⁿ⁻¹|∂*E.
```

Prove that the essential boundary differs from the reduced boundary by an `Hⁿ⁻¹`-null set
for locally finite-perimeter sets. Supply the converse finite-perimeter criterion for a
measurable set whose essential boundary has locally finite `Hⁿ⁻¹` measure. In particular,
establish `P(E) ≤ Hⁿ⁻¹(frontier E)` for measurable sets, as an extended-measure statement
with the appropriate local version. Its proof must include the boundary criterion; a
finite topological boundary measure is not an assumed smoothness hypothesis.

The proofs of blow-up, density estimates, covering, and rectifiability are G5 targets,
resting on G2–G4. Specifying a reduced-boundary predicate without proving the representation
theorem does not discharge this milestone.

## G6 — Traces, Gauss–Green, and classical domains

Construct the BV trace on bounded Lipschitz domains with the `Hⁿ⁻¹` boundary measure,
its boundedness estimate, interior approximate-limit characterization a.e., uniqueness,
locality, and agreement with PDE Lane A.6's Sobolev trace. Establish the extension operator,
zero-extension derivative formula including the boundary trace term, and gluing across
a Lipschitz interface. Use the boundary regularity and chart conventions of PDE A.6;
build missing surface-measure/chart comparisons using G2, rather than a second domain type.

Prove Gauss–Green for locally finite-perimeter sets and compactly supported `C¹` vector
fields, including localized forms and integrable noncompact-support extensions under
explicit hypotheses. For BV functions on Lipschitz domains give integration by parts
with the trace term. Compare outward normals and surface area for Lipschitz and `C¹`
domains with the classical graph formulas and DifferentialGeometry's Euclidean divergence
theorem. This comparison does not require manifold Stokes to construct the flat theory.

For the bounded region `Ω = TauCeti.filledHull C \ C` of a rectifiable Jordan curve,
prove finite perimeter and `P(Ω) = H¹(C)`. Explicitly prove the Jordan index theorem for
its closed simple AC arclength parametrization: for one sign `σ ∈ {−1,1}`, the existing
winding number equals `σ` on `Ω` and zero on the unbounded complementary component.
Identify that sign with orientation and prove its reversal and parametrization laws;
it is a conclusion, not a supplied hypothesis of Green's theorem.
The proof must establish the boundary normal and
measure comparison, using Jordan separation, G1–G5 and the AC boundary-integral identity
of DifferentialGeometry 5.6, with parametrization transport from G1. With `Jv = I*v`
and arclength unit tangent `τ`, identify the outward normal as `−σ Jτ` a.e. and the
corresponding signed boundary measure, so clockwise and counterclockwise curves both
give the same perimeter. This supplies
the genuine bridge from the measure-theoretic inequality to arbitrary rectifiable Jordan
curves; `frontier Ω = C` alone gives no equality of perimeter and curve length.

## Acceptance examples and completion

Compute derivative measures and perimeter for intervals, balls, boxes, and annuli; include
the endpoint atoms for a one-dimensional step function. Construct the Cantor–Lebesgue
function `C` on `[0,1]`, extended constantly outside that interval, from the ternary
Cantor-set/dyadic-value construction, using
Mathlib's Cantor set. Prove continuity, monotonicity, `C(0)=0`, `C(1)=1`, variation one,
and `C'=0` a.e.; its derivative measure is a singular continuous probability measure
supported on the Cantor set. This is the named singular BV example and the input to
Isoperimetry's non-AC homeomorphism example. Check complement invariance on the exterior of a ball, an infinite-volume
finite-perimeter set. Check null modification invariance on a punctured ball and on a
ball with a null dense subset added outside it; topological frontier and perimeter differ.
Compute the area formula for a graph and the multiplicity of a twice-traversed circle.
Give a rectifiable Jordan curve with a continuous non-AC parametrization and recover its
length, perimeter, and area through arclength. These exercise the APIs rather than replacing
the general theorems.

Completion requires all comparisons as well as all named theorems. Real-valued formulas
must establish integrability and finite measures before using `toReal` or a Bochner
integral. Null-set choices, chart choices, and parametrizations must disappear from the
final measures and geometric invariants.

## References and prior formalizations

- Francesco Maggi, [*Sets of Finite Perimeter and Geometric Variational Problems*](https://cvgmt.sns.it/paper/1880/):
  the perimeter, approximation, structure, and boundary framework.
- Leon Simon, [*Lectures on Geometric Measure Theory*](https://web.stanford.edu/class/math285/ts-gmt.pdf):
  rectifiability, tangential differentiation, and area/coarea.
- [MovingSofa](https://github.com/deancureton/MovingSofa) contains formalized Jordan-curve
  area and Hausdorff-length developments relevant to G1 and G6.
- The [Humanfia public source archive](https://huggingface.co/datasets/humanfia-lab/lean-eval-source/tree/main/problems/isoperimetric_inequality),
  [Jonathan Ho's isoperimetric development](https://github.com/hojonathanho/isoperimetric)
  (also [in LeanPool](https://github.com/LeanPool/lean-pool/tree/main/LeanPool/Isoperimetric)),
  and [kim-em/isoperimetric](https://github.com/kim-em/isoperimetric) are related formalizations;
  Isoperimetry describes their mathematical relation to the target.

These are sources of mathematical and API evidence, not required dependencies or prescribed
proofs. The targets are independently specified on top of Mathlib and Tau Ceti. Any use of
existing code follows the repository's coordination and attribution rules; completion is
judged against the intrinsic statements and reusable APIs above.
TauCetiRoadmap/HeightsAndUnits:
# Roadmap: heights, units and S-units of number fields

Dirichlet's unit theorem says that the units of a number field form a lattice of rank `r₁ + r₂ − 1`
modulo torsion, and Mathlib proves it. The height of an algebraic number says how large it is
arithmetically. This roadmap writes the dictionary between the two. A unit's height is the ℓ¹ norm
of its logarithmic embedding, up to the coordinate that embedding drops. The torsion units are
exactly the units of height one. The regulator is bounded above and below by products of heights
of a fundamental system, and the lower bound is sharp enough to choose a fundamental system of
controlled height. The roadmap then carries all of this to `S`-units. It proves the `S`-unit
theorem, builds the `S`-logarithmic lattice and defines the `S`-regulator.

Two pieces of geometry of numbers are needed on the way, and both are built here. The first is a
lattice **basis** controlled by the successive minima, not merely an independent family. The
second applies it to the kernel of an integer matrix. The result is a `ℤ`-**basis** of the integral
kernel of bounded sup norm, at the cost `k!/2^{k−1}` over the Bombieri–Vaaler bound for
independent vectors, with the gcd of the maximal minors. The roadmap also owns a small set of height
estimates that every consumer of heights needs and that no other roadmap supplies:
- the affine height of a tuple,
- bounds for values of linear forms and determinants,
- the `Northcott` instances for projective points and subspaces,
- the projective form of Kronecker's theorem,
- the lower bound for the height away from one at bounded degree.

"Done" means a contributor who needs a fundamental system of units of bounded height, an
`S`-unit group of known rank with an explicit fundamental system, a lattice basis inside dilates of
a convex body, or an integer kernel basis of bounded sup norm finds each one stated in its
natural generality, with its basic API, in Mathlib's vocabulary.

Suggested home: `TauCeti/NumberTheory/Height/` for Layers 0–1, beside the height foundation of
[DiophantineApproximationAndTranscendence](../DiophantineApproximationAndTranscendence/README.md);
`TauCeti/NumberTheory/GeometryOfNumbers/` for Layer 2; `TauCeti/NumberTheory/NumberField/Units/`
for Layer 3; and `TauCeti/RingTheory/DedekindDomain/SUnit.lean` with
`TauCeti/NumberTheory/NumberField/SUnits/` for Layer 4.

## Standing hypotheses and pinned conventions

Work over a field with `[Height.AdmissibleAbsValues K]` wherever the mathematics allows. Layers 0
and 1 are stated at that generality, except where an absolute height forces characteristic zero
or a number field. Layers 3 and 4 are about a number field `K` of degree `d = [K : ℚ]`, with
`r = NumberField.Units.rank K`. Tuples are indexed by an arbitrary finite type, never by `Fin n`
alone.

| Question | Convention |
| --- | --- |
| multiplicative or logarithmic | **Both** for every owned object. The multiplicative one is primary and `logX := Real.log (mulX)`, as in Mathlib. |
| relative or absolute | **Both, distinguished by name.** Over a fixed `K`, `Height.mulHeight` is relative. The absolute height carries the `abs` prefix (`NumberField.absMulHeight₁`) or is DAT's `absoluteProjectiveTupleHeight`. Layer 3 states its regulator bounds in the **absolute logarithmic** height `h = absLogHeight₁`, as Bugeaud–Győry do, and its comparisons with `logEmbedding` in the **relative** `logHeight₁`, which is `d · h`. |
| local factor at a place | `⨆ i, v (x i)`, written out, never wrapped in a definition. |
| the affine height | `Height.mulHeightAff x := Height.mulHeight (fun o : Option ι ↦ o.elim 1 x)`, the projective height of `(1, x)`. It is **not** scaling-invariant, and that is its whole purpose. |
| `S` | `S : Set (IsDedekindDomain.HeightOneSpectrum (𝓞 K))`, **finite places only**, with the infinite places always present. These are the carriers of `S.integer K` and `S.unit K`. The rank of `S.unit K` is `r + #S`. Bombieri–Gubler 1.5.10 instead includes the archimedean places in `S` and so writes the rank as `\|S\| − 1`. A contributor reading the book translates, and every statement here is in Mathlib's convention. |
| fundamental system | A family `ε : Fin r → (𝓞 K)ˣ` with `Subgroup.closure (Set.range ε) ⊔ torsion K = ⊤`, which is what Mathlib's `closure_fundSystem_sup_torsion_eq_top` says of `fundSystem K`. |
| ℓ¹ norm on `logSpace K` | Mathlib's `‖·‖` on the `Pi` type `logSpace K` is the **supremum** norm. Every ℓ¹ norm is written as `∑ w, |x w|`, and the sup-norm forms are separate statements. |
| declaration names | Statement-named, as in Mathlib. Siegel, Bombieri–Vaaler, Kronecker, Northcott and Dirichlet appear in docstrings, never in identifiers. The exception is a name that is the standard name of an object, such as `Northcott` the typeclass. |

## The build, in layers

### Layer 0: affine heights and the value bounds

**0.1 The affine height of a tuple.** Define
`Height.mulHeightAff (x : ι → K) := Height.mulHeight fun o : Option ι ↦ o.elim 1 x`, with
`logHeightAff` alongside, over any `[Height.AdmissibleAbsValues K]` and `[Finite ι]`. Prove:
- `1 ≤ mulHeightAff x`.
- `mulHeight x ≤ mulHeightAff x` and `mulHeight₁ (x i) ≤ mulHeightAff x`. The second fails for
  `mulHeight`.
- `mulHeightAff (x ∘ f) ≤ mulHeightAff x` for any `f`, with equality for a bijection.
- `mulHeightAff 0 = 1`.
- `mulHeightAff ![x] = mulHeight₁ x`, which is the test that the appended coordinate is the right
  one.
- The non-invariance as a theorem, `exists_mulHeightAff_smul_ne`: over `ℚ`, `![1]` and `![2]` have
  affine heights `1` and `2` and the same projective height.
- The bridge to DAT: for a number field `K` and `f : K →+* AlgebraicClosure ℚ`,
  `absoluteLogHeightAff (f ∘ x) = logHeightAff x / [K : ℚ]` for `x : Fin n → K`. DAT prepends the
  `1` with `Fin.cons`, and this layer appends it with `Option.elim`; the bridge is a reindexing.
(Bombieri–Gubler 1.5.)

**0.2 Values of linear forms and determinants.** Prove:
- `mulHeight₁ (∑ i, a i * x i) ≤ #ι ^ totalWeight K · mulHeightAff a · mulHeightAff x` for
  nonempty `ι`, with its logarithmic form. No bound in the projective heights of `a` and `x`
  exists, because `a ↦ c • a` scales the value and fixes `mulHeight a`.
- `mulHeight₁ A.det ≤ (#n)! ^ totalWeight K · ∏ j, mulHeightAff (fun i ↦ A i j)`, columnwise,
  from the Leibniz expansion and DAT §1.3's signed tuple sum bound
  `Height.mulHeight_sum_sign_comp_le`. Also the corollary `mulHeight₁ A.det ≤ (#n)! ^ totalWeight K · mulHeightAff (entries A) ^ #n`.
- The rejection test `exists_not_mulHeight₁_det_le`: a `1 × 1` matrix has `matrixMulHeight A = 1`
  and determinant its entry.
- Sharpness: `a = x = ![1, 1]` attains the linear-form constant.

**0.3 Arakelov bounds with constant one.** Over a number field, with DAT's `arakelovMulHeight`
applied to the tuple of entries `fun p : m × n ↦ A p.1 p.2`, prove:
- `arakelovMulHeight (fun j ↦ ∑ i, A (j, i) * x i) ≤ arakelovMulHeight A · arakelovMulHeight x`.
- `arakelovMulHeight (entries (A * B)) ≤ arakelovMulHeight (entries A) · arakelovMulHeight (entries B)`.
- Their logarithmic forms.

These need no `Nonempty` hypothesis and carry no cardinality. That is the contrast with DAT's
`matrixMulHeight_mul_le`, whose constant is `(card n) ^ totalWeight K` and which needs a nonempty
inner index. At an infinite place the local factor is the Frobenius norm, and Cauchy–Schwarz makes
it submultiplicative; at a finite place the ultrametric inequality does the same. The
linear-map bound is the one-column case of the matrix bound. Test: over `ℚ`, `A = [1 1]`,
`B = [[1, 0], [1, 1]]` give `matrixMulHeight (A B) = 2` against `matrixMulHeight A = matrixMulHeight B = 1`,
so the sup-norm constant `2 ^ totalWeight K` is attained, while the Arakelov bound holds with
constant `1`.

### Layer 1: Northcott instances and Kronecker's theorem

**1.1 Northcott on projective space.** Over a field with
`[Northcott (Height.mulHeight₁ (K := K))]`, prove `Northcott (Projectivization.mulHeight (K := K) (ι := ι))`
and the `logHeight` instance. Mathlib's `Mathlib/NumberTheory/Height/Northcott.lean` records both
as TODOs. The number-field instances then follow by instance resolution. Route:
- **Normalization.** `Projectivization.exists_rep_apply_eq_one_of_ne_zero` gives a representative
  with a chosen nonvanishing coordinate equal to `1`, and `exists_rep_apply_eq_one` is its
  corollary.
- **Coordinate bound.** `Height.mulHeight₁_div_le_mulHeight`, that
  `mulHeight₁ (x i / x j) ≤ mulHeight x`, is `Height.mulHeight_comp_le` along `![i, j]`.
- **Finiteness.** A bounded-height point is in the image of a finite set of normalized tuples.
  No ring of integers and no ideal norm enter.

There is **no** `Northcott` instance for `Height.mulHeight` on `ι → K`: the whole line `Kˣ • x` has
one height. (Hindry–Silverman B.2.3; Bombieri–Gubler 2.4.9 for `ℙⁿ`.)

**1.2 Northcott for subspaces.** Over a number field, `Northcott` instances for DAT's
`relativeSubspaceHeight`, `relativeSubspaceArakelovHeight` and `subspaceHeight`, and for their
logarithms, on `Submodule K (ι → K)` with **no rank condition**. Route:
- **Absolute height.** For `subspaceHeight` this is DAT's `finite_subspaceHeight_le`.
- **Relative Arakelov height.** `relativeSubspaceArakelovHeight = subspaceHeight ^ [K : ℚ]`, so
  its sublevel sets are those of `subspaceHeight`.
- **Relative sup height.** This needs the **reverse** comparison, because a bound on the smaller
  height must bound the larger one. Prove `relativeSubspaceArakelovHeight_le`: for
  `n = #ι` and `k = finrank K T`,
  `relativeSubspaceArakelovHeight T ≤ (n.choose k) ^ ([K : ℚ]/2) · relativeSubspaceHeight T`.
  It is the upper half of DAT's `arakelovMulHeight_sup_comparison` on the Plücker vector, whose
  index `Set.powersetCard ι k` has `n.choose k` elements and is nonempty because `k ≤ n`. Both
  heights are invariant under scaling, so the representative `relativePluckerPoint` picks does
  not matter. Bound `n.choose k ≤ 2 ^ n` uniformly. Then
  `{T | relativeSubspaceHeight T ≤ B}` lies inside
  `{T | relativeSubspaceArakelovHeight T ≤ 2 ^ (n [K : ℚ]/2) · B}`, which is finite by the
  previous item.
- **Logarithms.** These follow by `Northcott.comp_of_bddAbove` along `Real.log`, as Mathlib
  derives `Northcott (logHeight₁)`.

The rank-free statement is what the typeclass needs, because `Northcott h` quantifies over the
whole domain of `h`. The deliverable is the instance, through which `Northcott.exists_min_image`
produces a subspace of least height with a prescribed property.

**1.3 Kronecker's theorem and the height gap.** Over a field `F` of characteristic zero:
- **Kronecker.** For `x` integral over `ℚ`, `absMulHeight₁ x = 1 ↔ x = 0 ∨ ∃ n, 0 < n ∧ x ^ n = 1`,
  and `absLogHeight₁ x = 0 ↔ …`. The hard direction is DAT's `mahlerMeasure_eq_one_iff` through
  `mahlerMeasure_eq_absMulHeight₁_pow`. The easy direction is the power law
  `absMulHeight₁ (x ^ n) = absMulHeight₁ x ^ n` with `1 ≤ absMulHeight₁`.
- **Tuple power law.** `absoluteProjectiveTupleHeight (fun i ↦ x i ^ N) = absoluteProjectiveTupleHeight x ^ N`.
  It is local: `(⨆ i, v (x i))^N = ⨆ i, v (x i ^ N)`.
- **Projective Kronecker.** For a nonzero tuple `x` of algebraic coordinates,
  `absoluteProjectiveTupleHeight x = 1` if and only if every ratio `x i / x j` with `x j ≠ 0` is
  zero or a root of unity. The converse direction is a statement about tuples,
  `absoluteProjectiveTupleHeight_eq_one_of_forall_eq_zero_or_pow_eq_one`. Its proof: with `N` a
  common order of the nonzero coordinates, `x ^ N` has coordinates in `{0, 1}`, so it is its own
  square, and its height is an idempotent `≥ 1`. (Hindry–Silverman B.2.3.1.)
- **The gap.** `1 < absMulHeight₁ x` for `x` integral over `ℚ`, nonzero and not a root of unity.
  Also, for each `D`, `∃ c > 0` with `c ≤ absLogHeight₁ x` for every such `x` with
  `[ℚ⟮x⟯ : ℚ] ≤ D`. The proof is DAT's bounded-degree Northcott plus Kronecker, and the constant
  is **ineffective**: it is the minimum of a finite set. (Bombieri–Gubler 1.6.15.)
- **Refutation.** The dependence of `c` on `D` is essential: `2 ^ (1/N)` has
  `absLogHeight₁ = (log 2)/N`. State it as "for every `c > 0` there is such an `x` with height
  below `c`". The same family keeps `[ℚ(x):ℚ] · h(x) ≤ log 2`, so it does not bear on Lehmer's
  question.

### Layer 2: a basis from the minima, and Bombieri–Vaaler in the sup norm

**2.1 A basis from the minima** (Cassels, *An Introduction to the Geometry of Numbers*, Ch. V,
Lemma 8; Ch. I, Thm. I). Let `E` be a finite-dimensional real normed space, `L` a discrete
`Submodule ℤ E` and `B` a convex, symmetric set with nonempty interior.

*General form.* For any `ℝ`-independent `a : Fin n → E` with `a i ∈ L` and `n = finrank ℝ E`,
there is a `ℤ`-basis `b` of `L` with
`gauge B (b j) ≤ max (gauge B (a j)) ((∑ i ≤ j, gauge B (a i)) / 2)`. `IsZLattice ℝ L` is a
consequence, not a hypothesis. Route, by induction on `j`, with `V_j = span_ℝ {a i : i < j}`:
1. A basis of `L ∩ V_j` extends by one vector `y` to a basis of `L ∩ V_{j+1}`. This is GoN's
   §0.2.7 `saturated_adapted_basis_of_basis`, applied inside `V_{j+1}`.
2. Write `a j = c • y + w` with `c` a nonzero integer and `w ∈ L ∩ V_j`.
3. If `|c| = 1`, take `b j = c · a j`.
4. Otherwise replace `y` by `y − ∑ round(t_i) • a i`, where `y = c⁻¹ • a j + ∑ t_i • a i`. The
   result still extends the basis, and has gauge at most `½ gauge B (a j) + ½ ∑_{i<j} gauge B (a i)`.

The proof uses `gauge B (r • x) = |r| · gauge B x` for symmetric convex `B`, stated as
`gauge_smul_of_symmetric`. Over `ℝ` a convex symmetric set is balanced: for `x ∈ B` and
`|t| ≤ 1`, `t • x` lies on the segment from `-x` to `x`. Mathlib has no lemma saying so, so state
it as `balanced_of_convex_of_neg_mem`; then `gauge_smul_of_symmetric` is Mathlib's `gauge_smul`.

*Minima form.* In GoN's vocabulary: for `K : ConvexBody E` symmetric with `0 ∈ interior K` and `L`
a full lattice, there is a `ℤ`-basis `b` of `L` with
`b i ∈ (max 1 ((i + 1)/2) · successiveMin L K i) • K` for every `i : Fin (finrank ℝ E)`. Apply the
general form to GoN's `exists_successiveMin_witnesses`. This is strictly more than GoN's
`exists_integral_minimum_flag`, which bounds no vector of the basis.

Further requirements:
- The loss against Minkowski's second theorem is
  `∏_{i<n} max 1 ((i+1)/2) = n! / 2^{n−1}`. State it as `prod_max_one_add_one_div_two`.
- The `max` is forced at `i = 0`, where `λ_0` is attained.
- The general form needs no measure, no closedness and no boundedness. Those enter only in the
  minima form.

**2.2 Integral kernel bases and the minor gcd** (Bombieri–Vaaler 1983, Theorems 1 and 2;
Aliev–Henk 2023, §6; Cassels V Lemma 8). For an integer matrix `A : Matrix (Fin m) ι ℤ` whose rows
are linearly independent over `ℚ`, let `minorGcd A` be the gcd of its `m × m` minors, and let
`k = #ι − m` be the rank of the integral kernel `ker A = {x : ι → ℤ | A *ᵥ x = 0}`.

*Owned here.*
- **The arithmetic identity.**
  `minorGcd A · subspaceHeight (ker A) = √det(A Aᵀ)`, together with
  `linearIndependent_rows_rat_iff : rows independent over ℚ ↔ det(A Aᵀ) ≠ 0`, `0 < det(A Aᵀ)`
  and `1 ≤ minorGcd A`. This turns DAT §2.8's remark on the `K = ℚ` constant into a theorem.
- **Invariance.** `√det(A Aᵀ) / minorGcd A` is unchanged by `A ↦ U A` for `U ∈ GL_m(ℤ)`
  (`sqrt_det_div_minorGcd_unit_mul`, from `minorGcd_unit_mul` and the Gram determinant's
  `det U ^ 2 = 1`). Classical Siegel's bound `(#ι · max |A i j|)^{m/(#ι−m)}` moves under this
  substitution.
- **The geometric half.** For any lattice `L` in a subspace `V` of `EuclideanSpace ℝ ι`, with
  `cubeSlice V` the slice of `[−1, 1]^ι`, `∏ i, successiveMin L (cubeSlice V) i ≤ covolume L`.
  The `2^k` of GoN's `minkowski_second_upper` cancels the `2^k` of DAT's `siegelProductBallSlice`.
- **An integral kernel basis.** A `Module.Basis (Fin k) ℤ (ker A)`, so a basis of the whole
  integral kernel and not only of a sublattice of finite index, with
  `∏ l, (⨆ i, |b l i|) ≤ k!/2^{k−1} · √det(A Aᵀ) / minorGcd A`. At `k = 0` both sides are `1`.
- **Sharpness of Siegel's exponent.** The `m × (m+1)` system `B x_i = x_{i+1}` has every nonzero
  integer solution of sup norm at least `B^m`, against Siegel's bound `((m+1)B)^m`.

Assembly of the basis:
1. The covolume of `ℤ^ι ∩ ker A` in its real span equals `subspaceHeight (ker A)`. This is the
   `K = ℚ` case of DAT's `kernelLattice_covolume`.
2. The arithmetic identity rewrites it as `√det(A Aᵀ) / minorGcd A`. Its proof is DAT's
   `subspaceHeight_orthogonal`, which passes to the row space, and `plucker_cauchyBinet`, which
   computes the rows' Plücker norm as `√det(A Aᵀ)`.
3. The geometric half bounds the product of the minima of the cube slice by that covolume.
4. The minima form of 2.1 converts the minima into a basis. The cube slice's gauge is the sup
   norm, and the loss is `prod_max_one_add_one_div_two k = k!/2^{k−1}`.

*Adapters of DAT's `siegelKernelBasis`, not owned.* At `K = ℚ` DAT's theorem gives a `ℚ`-basis of
the kernel in `ℤ^ι` with `∏ Habs(x_l) ≤ H₂(rowSpace A)`. Dividing each vector by its content keeps
it in the kernel, keeps the family independent, and makes its sup norm equal to its height
(Mathlib's `Rat.mulHeight_eq_max_abs_of_gcd_eq_one`). With the arithmetic identity this is the
sup-norm form of Bombieri–Vaaler's Theorem 2: `ℤ`-independent `x : Fin k → (ι → ℤ)`, each primitive, with
`A *ᵥ x l = 0` and `∏ l, (⨆ i, |x l i|) ≤ √det(A Aᵀ) / minorGcd A`. Theorem 1 is the smallest
vector of that family: for `m < #ι` a nonzero `x` with
`⨆ i, |x i| ≤ (√det(A Aᵀ) / minorGcd A)^{1/k}`. State both as corollaries.

The independent family need **not** span `ker A`. For `A = [0, 0, 1]`, the vectors
`(1, 1, 0)` and `(1, −1, 0)` meet the bound `1`, but they span a sublattice of index `2` that misses
`(1, 0, 0)`. The basis milestone is therefore a separate statement, and its factor `k!/2^{k−1}` is
not to be dropped.

### Layer 3: heights of units and the regulator

Throughout, `K` is a number field, `w₀` and `logEmbedding` are Mathlib's
(`NumberField.Units.dirichletUnitTheorem`), and `u : (𝓞 K)ˣ`. Sums over `{w // w ≠ w₀}` use
`open scoped Classical`, since `InfinitePlace K` has no `DecidableEq`.

**3.1 The logarithmic embedding as a height** (Bombieri–Gubler 1.5.12; Bugeaud–Győry 1996, (12)).
The finite local factors of a unit are `1`, so:
- `logHeight₁ u = ∑ w, (mult w · log (w u))⁺`, the sum over all infinite places, which by the
  product formula is
- `2 · logHeight₁ u = ∑ w, |mult w · log (w u)|`.

These are the `S = ∅` case of DAT §4.5's identity and are cited from there. What this milestone
owns is the translation to `logEmbedding`, which drops the coordinate at `w₀`:
- `2 · logHeight₁ u = ∑_{w ≠ w₀} |logEmbedding u w| + |∑_{w ≠ w₀} logEmbedding u w|`.
- The two-sided bound `∑_{w ≠ w₀} |logEmbedding u w| ≤ 2 · logHeight₁ u ≤ 2 ∑_{w ≠ w₀} |logEmbedding u w|`.
- The sup-norm forms `‖logEmbedding u‖ ≤ 2 · logHeight₁ u` and
  `logHeight₁ u ≤ rank K · ‖logEmbedding u‖`.
- The absolute form `absLogHeight₁ u ≤ (∑_{w ≠ w₀} |logEmbedding u w|) / d`.
- Both tempting identities, as criteria. `logHeight₁ u = ∑_{w ≠ w₀} (logEmbedding u w)⁺` holds
  **iff `w₀ u ≤ 1`**, and `2 · logHeight₁ u = ∑_{w ≠ w₀} |logEmbedding u w|` holds **iff
  `w₀ u = 1`**.
- `finite_setOf_logHeight₁_le`: the units of bounded height are finite. This is Northcott along
  `(𝓞 K)ˣ → K`.

**3.2 Units of height one.**
- `absMulHeight₁ u = 1 ↔ u ∈ torsion K`, with the `mulHeight₁`, `logHeight₁` and `absLogHeight₁`
  forms. From 3.1, `2 · logHeight₁ u` is a sum of nonnegative terms and vanishes exactly when
  every `w u = 1`, which is Mathlib's `mem_torsion`.
- `logHeight₁ u = 0 ↔ logEmbedding u = 0`.
- Kronecker (1.3) removes the unit hypothesis: a nonzero `x : 𝓞 K` has `absMulHeight₁ x = 1` iff
  it has finite order. Such an `x` is a unit.
- Off the torsion the height is strictly above one, and no member of `fundSystem K` is torsion.
  Hence `0 < ∏ i, absLogHeight₁ (fundSystem K i)`.

**3.3 The regulator and the heights of a fundamental system** (Bugeaud–Győry 1996, Lemma 1, case
`S = S_∞`). Write `h = absLogHeight₁`.
- *Hadamard's bound, for every fundamental system* `ε`:
  `regulator K ≤ (2d)^r · ∏ i, h(ε i)`. Also `regOfFamily u ≤ (2d)^r · ∏ h(u i)` for any family,
  and the relative form `regulator K ≤ 2^r · ∏ logHeight₁ (ε i)`. Route: the rows of the
  `logEmbedding` matrix have ℓ¹ norm at most `2 · logHeight₁ = 2d · h` by 3.1, and
  `Matrix.abs_det_le_prod_sum_abs` bounds `|det M|` by the product of the ℓ¹ norms of the rows,
  over any linearly ordered field. For a fundamental system `regOfFamily ε = regulator K` is
  Mathlib's `regOfFamily_div_regulator` at index one. Also prove the positivity of `∏ h(ε i)` for
  every fundamental system.
- *A reduced fundamental system exists*: some fundamental system has
  `∏ i, h(ε i) ≤ (r!)² / (2^{r−1} d^r) · regulator K`, and it can be chosen to satisfy Hadamard's
  bound simultaneously. Route, which is Bugeaud–Győry's and produces exactly this constant:
  1. Let `logBall K = {x : logSpace K | ∑ w, |x w| ≤ 1}`. It is convex, symmetric, closed and
     bounded, and `volume (logBall K) = 2^r / r!` (`MeasureTheory.volume_sum_rpow_le` at `p = 1`;
     by hand at `r = 0`).
  2. Minkowski's upper bound gives `∏ λ_i ≤ r! · regulator K`. `logSpace K` carries the sup norm
     and is not an inner-product space, so state the adapter: transport `unitLattice K` and
     `logBall K` to `EuclideanSpace ℝ {w // w ≠ w₀}` along `WithLp.linearEquiv`. That map preserves
     volume, so it preserves the covolume (`ZLattice.covolume_comap`), and the minima are preserved
     by GoN's `successiveMin_linearEquiv`. Then apply GoN's `minkowski_second_upper`.
  3. Take the basis `b` of 2.1, which costs `r!/2^{r−1}`.
  4. Take units `ε i` with `logEmbedding ε i = b i`. They form a fundamental system because `b`
     spans `unitLattice K`, the whole image of `logEmbedding`
     (`closure_sup_torsion_eq_top_of_span`).
  5. Bound `h(ε i) ≤ (∑ w, |b i w|)/d` by 3.1.
- *Rank zero, as a check.* Both products are empty, and the two bounds agree with Tau Ceti's
  `NumberField.Units.regulator_eq_one_of_rank_eq_zero`, which is consumed and not reproved.

The reduced statement is existential and cannot be made for `fundSystem K` or for every fundamental
system once `r ≥ 2`: a unimodular change of basis then makes the heights arbitrarily large at fixed
regulator. In rank one `GL₁(ℤ) = {±1}`: the fundamental systems are `ζ ε^{±1}` with `ζ` torsion, and they
all have the same height. The
statement `∃ c₁ c₂ > 0, c₁ R ≤ ∏ h(ε_i) ≤ c₂ R` for a fixed field says nothing, so the constants
are part of the target.

### Layer 4: S-integers, the S-unit theorem and the S-regulator

**4.1 The height of an S-integer** (Bombieri–Gubler 1.5.10).
- *Dictionary.* For `v : HeightOneSpectrum (𝓞 K)` and `x : K`, `FinitePlace.mk v x ≤ 1 ↔
  v.valuation K x ≤ 1` and `FinitePlace.mk v x = 1 ↔ v.valuation K x = 1`. These are
  equivalences because the norm of a prime exceeds `1`. Consequently
  `Set.mem_integer_iff_finitePlace` and `Set.mem_unit_iff_finitePlace`.
- *Height identity.* For `x ∈ S.integer K`,
  `mulHeight₁ x = (∏ w : InfinitePlace K, max (w x) 1 ^ mult w) · ∏ᶠ v ∈ S, max (FinitePlace.mk v x) 1`.
  Also its logarithmic form, a `Finset` form, and the `S`-unit form derived in one line.
- *Characterization.* For `x ≠ 0`, the identity holds **iff** `x ∈ S.integer K`. A single finite
  place outside `S` where `|x|_v > 1` makes the full product strictly larger.
- *The case `S = ∅`.* `Set.mem_integer_empty_iff` (the algebraic integers) and
  `Set.mem_unit_empty_iff` (the units of `𝓞 K`), proved directly, so that the unit identity of
  3.1 is the `S = ∅` case of the display.
- *Tests.* The rational test is DAT §4.1's `mulHeight₁_sUnits_rat`. The rejection test is `1/2` at
  `S = ∅`: its infinite factor is `1` while its height is `2^d`.

**4.2 The S-unit theorem** (Bombieri–Gubler Theorem 1.5.13). Build it under the names and shapes
of mathlib4#40791, so that adopting that PR is a deletion plus an import:
- `Set.unitValuation : S.unit K →* (S → Multiplicative ℤ)`, `unitValuation_ker`, and
  `Set.unit_fg`.
- `Set.unit_finrank_numberField : finrank ℤ (Additive (S.unit K)) = Units.rank K + Nat.card S`
  for finite `S`.
- Beside it, the usable form in the shape of Mathlib's `exist_unique_eq_mul_prod`: a family
  `ε : Fin (rank K + #S) → S.unit K` such that every `S`-unit is uniquely `ζ · ∏ ε i ^ e i` with
  `ζ` torsion and `e` an integer vector.

Route:
1. The kernel of `unitValuation` is the image of `(𝓞 K)ˣ`, by 4.1's `S = ∅` statement. Its rank
   is Mathlib's `NumberField.Units.finrank_eq`.
2. The image has full rank `#S`. For each `v ∈ S`, the class of `v` has finite order in
   `ClassGroup (𝓞 K)`, and a generator of `v ^ orderOf [v]` is an `S`-unit with valuation nonzero
   at `v` and zero at the other places of `S` (`Set.exists_unitValuation_apply_ne_zero`). Only
   this torsion statement about the cokernel is needed. The class number is never computed and no
   map to the class group is built.
3. Rank–nullity over `ℤ`.

Build the fundamental system from the quotient of the `ℤ`-module `Additive (S.unit K)` by
`Submodule.torsion ℤ`, which is free, rather than from a quotient group.

**4.3 The S-logarithmic lattice and the S-regulator.** For a finite `S : Finset (HeightOneSpectrum (𝓞 K))`:
- Define `SUnit.logSpace S := ({w : InfinitePlace K // w ≠ w₀} ⊕ S) → ℝ`, and
  `SUnit.logEmbedding S` sending `x` to `mult w · log (w x)` on the left and
  `log (FinitePlace.mk v x)` on the right.
- Prove the product formula for `S`-units,
  `∑ w, mult w · log (w x) + ∑ v ∈ S, log (FinitePlace.mk v x) = 0`.
- Prove the `S`-analogue of 3.1 in `logEmbedding` coordinates:
  `2 · logHeight₁ x = ∑ |logEmbedding S x| + |∑ logEmbedding S x|`, with the two-sided and
  sup-norm comparisons. The rejection test `x = 2` at `S = ∅` is an `∅`-integer but not an
  `∅`-unit, and its sum is `d · log 2`.
- `logEmbedding S (unitOfUnits u) = Sum.elim (logEmbedding u) 0`.
- Define `SUnit.unitLattice S`, the image. Prove it is a **full lattice**:
  - **Discreteness** is Northcott: a bounded embedding is a bounded height by 4.1, and Mathlib's
    `NumberField.finite_setOfPred_logHeight₁_le` finishes (`SUnit.unitLattice_inter_ball_finite`).
  - **Spanning** is Mathlib's `unitLattice_span_eq_top` for the infinite coordinates together with
    the generators of 4.2 at the places of `S` (`SUnit.unitLattice_span_eq_top`).
- **The kernel.** `SUnit.logEmbedding_ker`: the kernel of `SUnit.logEmbedding S` is the torsion
  of `S.unit K`, as `(CommGroup.torsion (S.unit K)).toAddSubgroup`, the `S`-analogue of Mathlib's
  `logEmbedding_ker`. Route: if the kept coordinates vanish, the product formula makes the
  coordinate at `w₀` vanish too, so `logHeight₁ x = 0` by the height identity above, and
  Kronecker (1.3) makes `x` a root of unity. Equivalently, the kernel is the set of `S`-units of
  height one.
- **The quotient.** By the first isomorphism theorem, `SUnit.logEmbedding S` induces a `ℤ`-linear
  equivalence from the torsion-free quotient
  `Additive (S.unit K) ⧸ Submodule.torsion ℤ (Additive (S.unit K))` onto
  `SUnit.unitLattice S` (`SUnit.exists_quotTorsionEquiv_unitLattice`, sending the class of `x`
  to `logEmbedding S x`). It is the bridge from 4.2's quotient to 4.3's lattice.
- **Fundamental systems are bases.** A family `ε : ι → S.unit K` is a fundamental system, meaning
  `Subgroup.closure (Set.range ε) ⊔ CommGroup.torsion (S.unit K) = ⊤` with
  `#ι = rank K + #S`, **iff** `fun i ↦ logEmbedding S (Additive.ofMul (ε i))` is a `ℤ`-basis of
  `SUnit.unitLattice S` (`SUnit.isFundSystem_iff_basis`). The forward direction transports
  generation along the quotient equivalence. The converse lifts a basis to `S`-units and uses
  the kernel statement. In particular 4.2's fundamental system gives a basis.
- Define `SUnit.regulator S := ZLattice.covolume (SUnit.unitLattice S)` and prove
  `SUnit.regulator_pos`.
- **The determinant formula.** For a fundamental system `ε : ι → S.unit K`, an omitted infinite
  place `w'` and any `e : ι ≃ ({w // w ≠ w'} ⊕ S)`, `SUnit.regulator S` is the absolute
  determinant of the matrix whose row `i` is the weighted logarithms of `ε i` at the places
  `e`-indexed by its columns: `mult w · log (w (ε i))` at an infinite place and
  `log (FinitePlace.mk v (ε i))` at `v ∈ S` (`SUnit.regulator_eq_abs_det`). The generic `ι` and
  `e` carry the compatibility with reindexing. Independence of the basis is the
  `GL(ℤ)` invariance of `|det|`. Independence of `w'` is the product formula, which makes the
  columns sum to zero, so deleting any one column gives the same `|det|`. This is the
  `S`-analogue of Mathlib's `regulator_eq_det`, and it is how `regulator_empty` and the worked
  example are computed.
- Prove `SUnit.regulator_empty : SUnit.regulator ∅ = NumberField.Units.regulator K`. This is a
  theorem, not a definitional unfolding: `α ⊕ Empty` is not `α`. Transport the covolume along the
  measure-preserving linear equivalence of the two log spaces.
- **Rank.** `finrank ℤ (SUnit.unitLattice S) = rank K + #S`, from `ZLattice.rank`. Through the
  quotient equivalence, and because quotienting by torsion keeps the `ℤ`-rank, this is 4.2's
  `Set.unit_finrank_numberField`. The two routes must agree. `ZLattice.rank` alone computes only
  the rank of the image. The quotient equivalence is what makes it a statement about `S.unit K`.

## Worked examples (acceptance criteria)

- **Affine height.** `mulHeightAff ![1] = 1` and `mulHeightAff ![2] = 2` over `ℚ`, while
  `mulHeight ![1] = mulHeight ![2] = 1`.
- **Value bound.** Over `ℚ`, `a = x = ![1, 1]` gives `mulHeight₁ 2 = 2 = 2 ^ totalWeight ℚ · 1 · 1`.
- **Kronecker.** `absMulHeight₁ (-1 : ℚ) = 1`, `absMulHeight₁ (2 : ℚ) = 2`; the tuple
  `![1, -1]` has `absoluteProjectiveTupleHeight = 1` and `![1, 2]` has `2`.
- **Gap.** For every `c > 0` some `2 ^ (1/N)` has `absLogHeight₁` below `c`.
- **Basis from the minima.** For `L = ℤ⁵ + ℤ·(½,…,½)` and `K` the Euclidean unit ball, every
  minimum is `1`, attained by `e_0, …, e_4`, which span `ℤ⁵`, a sublattice of index `2`. So the
  minima witnesses are not a basis. 2.1 still produces a basis inside the bounds
  `max 1 ((i+1)/2)`, using `(½,…,½)`, of norm `√5/2 ≤ 5/2`, as its last vector.
- **Minor gcd.** The row `[1, 1]` has `det(AAᵀ) = 2`, `minorGcd = 1`, kernel generator
  `(1, −1)` of sup norm `1 ≤ √2`. The row `[2, 2]` has `det = 8`, `minorGcd = 2` and the same bound
  `√2`. This tests rational rescaling of a row, not a unimodular change.
- **Unimodular shear.** `A = [[1, 0, −1], [0, 1, −1]]` has Gram determinant `3`, minors `1, −1, 1`
  and `minorGcd = 1`, so the bound is `√3`. The kernel is generated by `(1, 1, 1)`, of sup norm `1`.
  The shear `U = [[1, 1], [0, 1]]` gives `U A = [[1, 1, −2], [0, 1, −1]]`, again with Gram
  determinant `3` and minors `1, −1, 1`. Classical Siegel's bound moves from `3^2 = 9` to
  `6^2 = 36`.
- **Independent family against basis.** For `A = [0, 0, 1]`, `(1, 1, 0)` and `(1, −1, 0)` meet
  the bound `1` and span a sublattice of index `2` in `ker A = ℤ² × 0`. The basis milestone
  returns `(1, 0, 0), (0, 1, 0)`, inside its bound `2!/2 · 1 = 1`.
- **Regulator, sharp at `ℚ(√2)`.** `r = 1`, `d = 2`, `ε = 1 + √2`, and
  `regulator = log(1+√2)` by Mathlib's `regulator_eq_det` at rank one,
  `h(ε) = log(1+√2)/2`. Hadamard: `log(1+√2) ≤ 4 · log(1+√2)/2`. Reduced:
  `log(1+√2)/2 ≤ (1/2) · log(1+√2)`, an **equality**, so the constant `(r!)²/(2^{r−1} d^r)` cannot
  be lowered at `r = 1, d = 2`.
- **Rank zero.** For `ℚ` and every imaginary quadratic field, both bounds of 3.3 have empty
  products and agree with Tau Ceti's `regulator_rat_eq_one` and
  `regulator_eq_one_of_isTotallyComplex_of_finrank_eq_two`.
- **S-units over `ℚ`.** `S = {2}`: rank `0 + 1 = 1`, fundamental system `{2}`, torsion `{±1}`,
  `SUnit.regulator S = log 2` by the determinant formula: the `1 × 1` matrix at the place `2`
  is `log |2|_2 = −log 2`. The element `1/2` is in `S.unit ℚ`, and its height `2` is carried at
  `2`.

## Ordering

Layer 0 first: 0.1 is used by 0.2, which also uses DAT §1.3's tuple sum bound. Layer 1 needs
only Layer 0's normalization lemmas and DAT §§0.2–0.3, 2.5. Layer 2 needs GoN §§0.2, 1.2, 1.5 and

`S = ∅` identity as a check; 4.2 needs 4.1; 4.3 needs 4.1, 4.2, 3.1 and Kronecker (1.3). The
headline milestones are 3.3, 4.2 and 4.3.
